vulns.description: Authlib is a Python library which builds OAuth and OpenID Connect servers. Prior to 1.9.0, OpenIDMixin.parse_id_token() reads the nonce_supported decision from the untrusted ID token being validated and sets the expected nonce to null when that claim is the JSON boolean false. In implicit and hybrid relying parties, or applications that directly accept externally supplied ID tokens, an attacker with a captured validly signed token can bypass the nonce-to-session binding and replay the victim's token into an attacker-controlled session. Plain authorization code flow is not affected, and the token must still pass signature, issuer, and audience validation. OpenIDMixin.parse_id_token() trusts nonce_supported in both authlib/integrations/base_client/sync_openid.py and authlib/integrations/base_client/async_openid.py to disable the expected nonce. This issue is fixed in version 1.9.0.

Authlib is a Python library which builds OAuth and OpenID Connect servers. Prior to 1.9.0, OpenIDImplicitGrant.validate_authorization_request() checks the client-controlled raw request.payload.scope for openid after the parent grant has filtered allowed scopes into request.scope. A registered client permitted an ID token response type but not the openid scope can add openid to the request, obtain user consent, and receive a signed ID token containing the user's subject and allowed profile claims. Authorization code flow and deployments that allow openid for every client permitted an ID token response are not affected. In authlib/oidc/core/grants/implicit.py, OpenIDImplicitGrant.validate_authorization_request() checks request.payload.scope instead of the filtered request.scope. This issue is fixed in version 1.9.0.

Authlib is a Python library which builds OAuth and OpenID Connect servers. Prior to 1.9.0, the default RFC 7523 JWTBearerGrant.get_audiences() returns an empty list, causing JWTBearerGrant.verify_claims() to require only that an aud claim exists without matching the current authorization server. An attacker holding a legitimate assertion for another service can present it to a server that shares the signing key and uses the default grant, obtaining an access token across a trust boundary. Implementations that override get_audiences() with the server's valid audience identifiers are not affected. This issue is fixed in version 1.9.0.

Authlib is a Python library which builds OAuth and OpenID Connect servers. From 1.3.1 until 1.9.0, OctKey.import_key() checks asymmetric-key markers only at byte zero while Authlib's PEM loaders accept leading whitespace, comments, or a byte-order mark. In deployments that use the documented mixed algorithm registry and already configure verification with PEM or certificate bytes containing such a prefix, an unauthenticated attacker who knows those same public-key bytes can use them as an HMAC secret and forge HS256 tokens with arbitrary identity or authorization claims. This is a bypass of the remediation for CVE-2024-37568. The module-level jwt object reaches OctKey.import_key() in authlib/jose/rfc7518/oct_key.py, where POSSIBLE_UNSAFE_KEYS fails to identify prefixed asymmetric key material. This issue is fixed in version 1.9.0.

Authlib is a Python library which builds OAuth and OpenID Connect servers. Prior to 1.9.0, Authlib's RFC 9101 JWTAuthenticationRequest passes the unauthenticated, client-controlled request_uri parameter to the abstract get_request_object() hook before applying a destination or registration policy; the hook itself performs no network request, while the documentation demonstrates an unrestricted HTTP fetch. In deployments whose integrator implements that hook as an unrestricted outbound fetch, a remote attacker who knows a valid public client identifier can make the authorization server request internal, link-local, or otherwise unintended URLs and can distinguish fetch outcomes through different error responses and timing. Deployments whose custom hook already applies a secure allowlist, destination controls, and retrieval limits are not affected. The JWTAuthenticationRequest implementation in authlib/oauth2/rfc9101/authorization_server.py forwards request_uri to get_request_object() before an application-approved retrieval policy accepts the destination. This issue is fixed in version 1.9.0.

Authlib is a Python library which builds OAuth and OpenID Connect servers. Prior to 1.9.1, Authlib's OctKey.import_key() and HMAC signing and verification path accept zero-length key material. If an application's secret lookup can return an empty string or empty bytes, a remote attacker can compute the deterministic HS256, HS384, or HS512 signature for arbitrary token claims and have Authlib treat the token as authentic. This issue is fixed in version 1.9.1.

Authlib is a Python library which builds OAuth and OpenID Connect servers. From 0.13 until 1.8.0, authlib.common.security.is_secure_transport() uses a textual prefix comparison for loopback HTTP exemptions, so a URL whose userinfo begins with a loopback host can be accepted even when its parsed host is an external non-loopback system. An external party able to supply a URL to OIDC RP-Initiated Logout registration, authorization-server metadata validation, or another call site can bypass the TLS-required guard and cause cleartext redirection or acceptance of cleartext endpoints. The issue does not bypass redirect URI exact matching and does not by itself forge tokens or authenticate users. The vulnerable authlib.common.security.is_secure_transport() implementation in authlib/common/security.py misinterprets the userinfo component before OIDC RP-Initiated Logout dynamic client registration and other consumers enforce transport security. This issue is fixed in version 1.8.0.

Authlib (prior to 1.9.0) contains a signature verification bypass vulnerability. The JsonWebSignature.deserialize_json() method accepts a JSON Serialization JWS object and returns the payload as successfully verified without checking for a signature and without requiring a cryptographic key.  ## Root cause  `authlib/jose/rfc7515/jws.py`, read on the installed 1.8.0 artifact:  ```python is_valid = True                        # set before anything is checked for header_obj in obj["signatures"]:   # empty array means the body never runs     jws_header, valid = self._validate_json_jws(...)     if not valid:         is_valid = False ... if is_valid:     return rv                          # returns the payload as verified ```  `is_valid` is initialised to `True` and only ever set to `False` from inside the loop. A JWS JSON Serialization object whose `signatures` array is empty iterates zero times, so the flag survives and the payload is returned as successfully verified. No key is consulted, because no signature is examined.  ## Reproduction  ```python import base64 from authlib.jose import JsonWebSignature  def b64(b):     return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(b).rstrip(b"=").decode()  jws = JsonWebSignature() payload = b'{"sub":"attacker","role":"admin"}' forged = {"payload": b64(payload), "signatures": []}  print(jws.deserialize_json(forged, key=None)) ```  Observed on authlib 1.8.0, Python 3.14, clean virtualenv:  ``` [A] ATTACK   general JSON, signatures:[] , key=None     ACCEPTED  -> {'header': [], 'payload': b'{"sub":"attacker","role":"admin"}'} [B] ATTACK   general JSON, signatures:[] , key=<real key>     ACCEPTED  -> {'header': [], 'payload': b'{"sub":"attacker","role":"admin"}'} [C] CONTROL+ genuine general JSON with 2 signatures, right key     ACCEPTED (expected) payload= b'{"sub":"attacker","role":"admin"}' [D] CONTROL- same object, first signature corrupted     rejected (expected): BadSignatureError bad_signature: [E] CONTROL- signatures array removed entirely (not empty, absent)     rejected: DecodeError Missing "protected" value: ```  [C] proves the verifier works normally on a genuine object, so a deployment looks healthy. [D] proves tampering is caught. [E] proves this is specifically the empty-array case and not a general missing-member bug. [A] and [B] are the bypass, and [B] shows that holding the correct key does not save a caller: the empty array is accepted either way.  For comparison, joserfc 1.7.5, the library this module's deprecation warning points users to, rejects the identical object with `BadSignatureError`. The correct behaviour already exists in your newer library.  ## Impact  Any relying party that calls `JsonWebSignature.deserialize_json()` on input it did not produce will accept an attacker-authored payload as signed. Where that payload carries identity or authorisation claims, this is a complete authentication bypass by an unauthenticated remote caller with no key material.   ## What would fix it  In `_deserialize_json`, reject an empty `signatures` array before the loop, or initialise the flag from the signature count, for example `is_valid = len(obj["signatures"]) > 0`. Pull request #938 proposes the same thing.

## Description  ### Summary  RFC 7592 (OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration Management Protocol) lets a previously registered client read, update, or delete its own registration, authenticated by a `registration_access_token` issued specifically to that client at registration time. The entire security model of this protocol depends on the server verifying that the token presented in the request actually belongs to the client identified in the request, not merely that the token is valid for some client.  Authlib's `ClientConfigurationEndpoint` implements the control flow correctly in structure, calling `authenticate_token`, then `authenticate_client`, then `check_permission`, and treats all three as abstract methods that "Developers MUST implement in subclass." The problem is that the documented example implementations for these methods, taken together exactly as written, never perform the one check that matters: binding the authenticated token to the specific client being accessed. A developer who implements these methods by following the provided examples ends up with a complete authorization bypass on this endpoint.  ### Details  `authenticate_client`'s documented example (`authlib/oauth2/rfc7592/endpoint.py`):  ```python def authenticate_client(self, request):     """Read a client from the request payload.     Developers MUST implement this method in subclass::          def authenticate_client(self, request):             client_id = request.payload.data.get("client_id")             return Client.get(client_id=client_id)      :return: client instance     """     raise NotImplementedError() ```  This looks the target client up purely by the `client_id` supplied in the request payload, with no reference to the token at all.  `check_permission`'s documented example, in the same file:  ```python def check_permission(self, client, request):     """Checks whether the current client is allowed to be accessed, edited     or deleted. Developers MUST implement it in subclass, e.g.::          def check_permission(self, client, request):             return client.editable      :return: boolean     """     raise NotImplementedError() ```  This checks a property of the target client alone (whether it is generally "editable"), again with no reference to `request.credential`, the authenticated token object returned earlier by `authenticate_token` and stored on the request specifically so that later steps can check it:  ```python def create_configuration_response(self, request):     token = self.authenticate_token(request)     if not token:         raise AccessDeniedError()      request.credential = token      client = self.authenticate_client(request)     ...     if not self.check_permission(client, request):         raise UnauthorizedClientError(...) ```  `request.credential` is set specifically so that a binding check can be performed downstream, but neither documented example ever reads it. Following both examples as written produces an implementation where the only requirements to access, modify, or delete a client's registration are: possessing any valid registration_access_token for any client, and knowing or guessing the target `client_id`.  This is meaningfully different from how the equivalent example is written for the token introspection endpoint (RFC 7662) elsewhere in the same codebase, which does correctly demonstrate checking the authenticated caller's own identity (`authlib/oauth2/rfc7662/introspection.py`):  ```python def check_permission(self, token, client, request):     """Check if the request has permission to introspect the token. Developers     MUST implement this method::          def check_permission(self, token, client, request):             # only allow a special client to introspect the token             return client.client_id == "introspection_client"     """ ```  In that endpoint, `client` represents the already-authenticated caller (verified through normal client credential authentication earlier in the flow), so checking a property of `client` is meaningful authorization logic. In the RFC 7592 endpoint, `client` instead represents the target being acted upon, not the caller, so the same style of example is actively misleading: it looks like a reasonable authorization check but performs none of the binding the protocol requires.  No file anywhere in the repository, including the Flask, Django, and SQLAlchemy integration modules, provides a complete, corrected reference implementation of `ClientConfigurationEndpoint`. The misleading docstring examples are the only guidance shipped for this endpoint.  ### Realistic exploitability  RFC 7591 dynamic client registration is commonly deployed without requiring an initial access token, since the specification explicitly anticipates open, self-service registration as a normal deployment model. Under that common configuration, an attacker can freely self-register their own throwaway client with no authentication at all, receive a valid `registration_access_token` scoped to that throwaway client, and then present that same token against `/register/{target_client_id}` for any other client, since neither documented example checks that the token corresponds to the target. If the target client's `editable` property (or whatever equivalent the developer implements based on the documented example) is true, an attacker can read the victim client's full registration including its metadata, update it (for example, changing `redirect_uris` to an attacker-controlled endpoint, enabling authorization code or token interception against that client's users), or delete it outright.  ### Reproduction  1. Deploy an authorization server using `ClientConfigurationEndpoint` with `authenticate_client` and `check_permission` implemented exactly as documented in the class's own docstrings. 2. As an attacker, register a new client via the RFC 7591 registration endpoint (commonly open/anonymous), obtaining `client_id_A` and `registration_access_token_A`. 3. Identify or guess `client_id_B`, belonging to a different, unrelated client. 4. Send `GET /register/client_id_B` (or `PUT`/`DELETE`) with `Authorization: Bearer registration_access_token_A`, and `client_id` set to `client_id_B` in the request body for the `PUT` case. 5. `authenticate_token` succeeds because `registration_access_token_A` is a valid token. `authenticate_client` succeeds because it looks up `client_id_B` directly from the payload, ignoring which token was presented. `check_permission` succeeds because it only checks `client_B.editable`, not whether `registration_access_token_A` has any relationship to `client_B`. The request proceeds and returns, modifies, or deletes client B's registration.  ### Impact  Full read, modify, and delete access to any other client's registration record, for any party able to obtain a valid registration_access_token for any client of their own. In an open dynamic registration deployment this reduces to no meaningful barrier at all, since attackers can self-issue their own qualifying token for free. Impact includes disclosure of client metadata, redirect URI hijacking enabling authorization code or token interception, and denial of service via deletion of arbitrary client registrations.  ## Suggested fix  Update the documented example for `check_permission` (or `authenticate_client`) to explicitly demonstrate binding the authenticated token to the target client, for example:  ```python def check_permission(self, client, request):     return request.credential.client_id == client.get_client_id() ```  and add an explicit warning in both docstrings that omitting this comparison results in a complete authorization bypass on this endpoint. Consider also shipping a complete, correct reference implementation of `ClientConfigurationEndpoint` in the Flask/Django/SQLAlchemy integration modules, since none currently exists.  ---  ## Affected products  **Ecosystem:** pip   **Package name:** Authlib   **Affected versions:** 1.7.2   **Patched versions:** 1.9.1  ## Severity  Privileges Required is Low, reflecting that the attacker needs some registration_access_token of their own, which under the common open dynamic registration deployment model is trivially self-issued. This is a documentation/reference-implementation issue rather than a bug the library enforces unconditionally on every deployment, since `authenticate_client` and `check_permission` are abstract methods a developer must implement; the finding is that the only guidance provided for implementing them correctly is, itself, exploitable if followed as written.

CVE-2026-111497 ("Node2Shell") is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) in Google's Brotli decoder (c/dec/decode.c). DecodeBlockTypeAndLength() returns an ambiguous value for an invalid block switch, and the fast decode path discards it (CWE-252, unchecked return value), so a crafted Brotli stream makes the decoder continue on corrupted state and write past the ring buffer. Upstream rates it CVSS 4.0 9.2 and classifies the impact as potential remote code execution.  The vulnerability is in Google's C library, not in Node.js specifically. The PyPI `Brotli` package is Google's CPython binding and compiles the same c/dec/decode.c that has the actual vulnerability. All `Brotli` releases up to and including 1.2.0 ship the vulnerable decoder; 1.2.1 contains the upstream fix (commit 0ed4268a) and differs from 1.2.0 only in that fix plus a version bump.  The decoder is reached whenever untrusted Brotli data is decompressed. With `Brotli` installed, common HTTP clients decode Brotli responses automatically (urllib3/requests, httpx with the brotli extra, aiohttp) and services that accept `Content-Encoding: br` request bodies decode inbound data, so the flaw is reachable from attacker-controlled input.

Certifi versions before 2026.10.18 include the `emSign ECC Root CA - G3` root certificate in their bundled CA store. Eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates that chain to this root have compromised private keys and the CA has revoked them.   An attacker with one of the compromised keys can issue valid-looking certificates for any hostname. If the attacker is also on-path, they can intercept or modify TLS traffic from clients that trust the certifi bundle. Examples include `requests`, `urllib3` and `pip`, and the Python.org macOS installer.  Certifi 2026.10.18 removed all emSign roots from the bundle. Certifi 2026.10.19 restored the emSign roots that are not affected. Upgrade to 2026.10.19 or later, and rebuild container images that vendor certifi.

filelock on Windows ignores the `mode` argument. `FileLock(path, mode=0o600)` creates the same file as `FileLock(path)`: one with no security descriptor of its own (the Windows record that says who may access a file). Its access list, or ACL, is whatever the lock directory hands down to new files. filelock creates the `ReadWriteLock` database, which it asks to be `0o600`, the same way. In a directory whose inheritable ACL grants other local accounts access to new files, those accounts can open the lock file or database. They can take the byte-range lock (a lock on a span of bytes in a file) once the owner releases it and keep the owner's later `acquire()` calls waiting or timing out. They can read holder metadata an `on_acquired` hook left in a `preserve_lock_file=True` file. Where the directory hands down modify access, they can write to both files.  `lock.mode` still reports `0o600`. The documentation neither promises an ACL on Windows nor says that Windows drops the mode. On Unix the same mode keeps other accounts out. Mutual exclusion between processes that follow the protocol holds on either platform. Affected versions are filelock 3.10.0 through 4.2.0 on Windows.  Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private. Finding covered by this advisory:  - `ANT-2026-0KEO0DDO` [medium, CWE-732]: WindowsFileLock ignores mode; 0o600 lock files inherit the directory ACL.  ## Severity  **CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:L` scores 5.3 (Medium).**  `AV:L` (local): the other account needs a logon on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:L` (low attack complexity): no race. `C:L` (partial confidentiality impact): the lock file (holder metadata) and the lock database are readable where `0o600` was meant to keep them private. `I:L` (partial integrity impact): in the directory layout the maintainers tested, the other account can also write both files, which lets it corrupt the lock's own state but nothing the lock protects. `A:L` (partial availability impact): the other account can hold the byte-range lock and make the owner wait or time out. `S:U` (scope unchanged).  Classification from the review: **Windows permission failure with security impact only where callers rely on `mode=0o600` across accounts**. The review had marked it an unconfirmed Windows claim, since the scanner traced stand-in Win32 calls on Linux. The maintainers have since confirmed it on Windows with two local accounts (see Evidence). The scanner rated this medium; the maintainers keep medium.  ## Scope and preconditions  - The affected classes are `FileLock` and `AsyncFileLock` on Windows (`WindowsFileLock`), and the SQLite database of `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock`. Both go through `_open_non_reparse_fd`. The soft locks create their markers with `os.open`, which also keeps only a read-only bit of the mode on Windows; the scanner did not examine them further. - The directory is one that other local accounts cannot write, which the documentation already requires on Windows, but whose inheritable entries grant them read (or modify) access to new files. Examples are a service's data directory readable by `Users`, or any directory with `(OI)(CI)` entries (entries that new files and sub-directories inherit) for another account. A directory whose ACL already excludes other accounts, such as one inside a user profile, hides the problem. - The other account must open the file. According to the `LockFileEx` documentation, read access is enough to take the byte-range lock, so it can hold the lock whenever the owner does not. The lock file exists while the owner holds the lock, and stays after release with `preserve_lock_file=True`. The `ReadWriteLock` database is not unlinked at any point. - Unix is not affected, because `UnixFileLock` creates the file with the mode and repeats it with `fchmod`. Mutual exclusion between cooperating processes is not affected.  ## Affected code  Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: [`_open_non_reparse_fd` reduces the mode to one `read_only` bit](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_windows.py#L252-L253). That bit is false for every accepted mode, because [`_check_mode`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_api.py#L526) rejects any mode without owner read and write, and an unset mode becomes `0o666`. In [`_nt_open`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_windows.py#L283-L310) the `OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES.SecurityDescriptor` field stays unassigned, and `read_only` only chooses `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_READONLY`. [`_open_lock_database`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1079-L1086) passes `0o600` through the same function on Windows.  ## Introduced  [d0061e4](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/d0061e4643df) "added multiuser support and associated tests" ([#192](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/192), 2023-03-15), first tag 3.10.0 (verified), added the `mode` parameter and on Windows handed it to `os.open`, which applies only the read-only attribute. The Windows backend has applied no more of the mode than that at any version, so this is a long-standing gap rather than a regression.  ## Mechanism  `_open_non_reparse_fd(path, mode)` computes `read_only = not mode & _OWNER_WRITE` and calls `_nt_open(path, read_only=read_only)`. `_nt_open` fills an `OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES` with the NT path and `OBJ_CASE_INSENSITIVE` and leaves `SecurityDescriptor` NULL. It then calls `NtCreateFile` with `FILE_OPEN_IF` and `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL` (or `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_READONLY` when `read_only`, which no accepted mode produces). Nothing consults the group and other bits. Per the `NtCreateFile` and `OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES` documentation, a NULL descriptor gives the new file default security, which on NTFS is the set of inheritable entries of the parent directory. A lock file created with `mode=0o600` in a directory that hands down read access to `Users` is therefore readable by `Users`.  Nothing tells the caller. The constructor validates the mode, `lock.mode` returns `0o600`, and `has_explicit_mode` is `True`. `docs/concepts.rst` says "filelock creates the file with it" and that "`0o600` and `0o700` keep other UIDs out", with no Windows caveat. Only the `_open_non_reparse_fd` docstring and a comment in `_soft.py` record the limitation.  ## Reproduction  The scanner's reproducer for `ANT-2026-0KEO0DDO`, quoted as received. It ran against commit `b831496b0273`.  **`repro`**  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 import os import shutil import subprocess import sys import tempfile  private_job = "/tmp/repro.d/job_with_private_lock.py"  # with FileLock(path, mode=0o600) default_job = "/tmp/repro.d/job_with_default_lock.py"  # with FileLock(path) on_windows_backend = "/tmp/repro.d/run_on_windows_backend.py"  # prints every Win32 call filelock makes  os.umask(0o022) locks = tempfile.mkdtemp()  # control: UnixFileLock, which leaves the lock file behind subprocess.run([sys.executable, private_job, f"{locks}/private.lock"], check=True) subprocess.run([sys.executable, default_job, f"{locks}/default.lock"], check=True) unix_private_mode = os.stat(f"{locks}/private.lock").st_mode & 0o777 unix_default_mode = os.stat(f"{locks}/default.lock").st_mode & 0o777  # trigger: the same two programs on WindowsFileLock, same lock name so the call lists can be compared whole windows_private = [sys.executable, on_windows_backend, private_job, f"{locks}/job.lock"] windows_default = [sys.executable, on_windows_backend, default_job, f"{locks}/job.lock"] windows_private_calls = subprocess.run(windows_private, check=True, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.splitlines() windows_default_calls = subprocess.run(windows_default, check=True, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.splitlines() shutil.rmtree(locks)  # check: mode=0o600 must reach the OS; on Windows that means a security descriptor on NtCreateFile print(f"CONTROL  UnixFileLock FileLock(path, mode=0o600): lock file mode {unix_private_mode:#o}") print(f"CONTROL  UnixFileLock FileLock(path):             lock file mode {unix_default_mode:#o}") for call in windows_private_calls:     print(f"OBSERVED WindowsFileLock FileLock(path, mode=0o600): {call}") for call in windows_default_calls:     print(f"OBSERVED WindowsFileLock FileLock(path):             {call}") print(f"OBSERVED the two Win32 call lists are identical: {windows_private_calls == windows_default_calls}")  honoured_on_unix = unix_private_mode == 0o600 and unix_default_mode == 0o644 private_create = next(call for call in windows_private_calls if call.startswith("NtCreateFile(")) dropped_on_windows = (     "ObjectAttributes.SecurityDescriptor=None" in private_create     and windows_private_calls == windows_default_calls ) print("BUG" if honoured_on_unix and dropped_on_windows else "OK") ```  **`repro.d/job_with_default_lock.py`**  ```python import sys  from filelock import FileLock  with FileLock(sys.argv[1]):     pass ```  **`repro.d/job_with_private_lock.py`**  ```python import sys  from filelock import FileLock  with FileLock(sys.argv[1], mode=0o600):     pass ```  **`repro.d/run_on_windows_backend.py`**  ```python import ctypes import fcntl import os import runpy import sys import types  # Stand-ins for the ntdll, kernel32 and msvcrt functions filelock's Windows backend calls. A hard link is a second name for the same file. With a mode such as `0o666` the file, still owned by the lock user, also becomes readable and writable by that other user. ### Summary   `create_submodule(name, path, url)` clones a submodule into the repo's own `.git` directory before it rejects the path. A `path` of ".git/hooks" is accepted by the pre-clone check, so the submodule is cloned straight into the live hooks directory, and a file named `post-checkout` in the submodule becomes an executable `.git/hooks/post-checkout`. On 3.2.0+ the later index check does raise `ValueError`, but only after the clone already wrote to disk, and it does not remove the planted hook; on 3.1.x there is no such check and the call succeeds silently. Either way the hook runs on the next git operation (e.g. checkout), giving code execution.  ### Details   The checkout path is validated too late, after the clone has already mutated disk. This breaks the "validate before mutation" invariant that commit 43a43cd8 ("Validate submodule checkout and metadata paths before mutation") set out to enforce. ## Summary  `Remote.pull()` in GitPython forwards its positional `refspec` argument directly to the `git pull` child process while its unsafe-option guard inspects only keyword arguments. An application that passes attacker-influenced data as the `refspec` (for example a user-supplied branch or refspec parameter in a web or CI service) can supply an option-shaped value such as `--upload-pack=<command>`. The value bypasses the `unsafe_git_pull_options` check, is placed after the `--` separator on the `git pull` command line, and is executed as the upload-pack program for local-path or SSH transports. This yields arbitrary command execution with the privileges of the calling process using the documented default arguments (`allow_unsafe_options=False`).  ## Root Cause  `Remote.pull()` is documented to reject dangerous options unless `allow_unsafe_options=True`, and `--upload-pack` is explicitly listed as such an option. The guard, however, only screens keyword arguments and never the positional `refspec`. The check builds its candidate list with `Git._option_candidates([], kwargs)`, passing an empty list in place of the positionals, so the `refspec` value is never compared against `unsafe_git_pull_options = ["--upload-pack"]`. The normalized `refspec` is then forwarded verbatim to the `git pull` invocation. The leading `--` separator that neutralizes an option-shaped refspec for `git fetch` and `git push` does not protect `git pull`, because `git pull` re-forwards its trailing positionals to an internal `git fetch` without re-inserting a `--` separator, so the positional becomes an option to that internal fetch.  ```text Affected function: git.remote.Remote.pull Source: git/remote.py (guard at the check_unsafe_options call using _option_candidates([], kwargs); sink at the self.repo.git.pull("--", self, refspec, ...) invocation) ```  ## Impact  An attacker who controls the `refspec` value passed to `Remote.pull()` achieves arbitrary operating-system command execution as the process invoking GitPython, with no additional privileges and no user interaction, on the default code path. Exploitation requires that the pulled remote uses a transport that runs upload-pack on the local side, namely a local filesystem path or SSH; over HTTPS the `--upload-pack` value is inert because the server ignores a client-supplied upload-pack program. This transport requirement narrows the population of vulnerable deployments but does not add work for the attacker once a vulnerable target is reached. Working checkouts commonly use local-path or SSH origins, so the exposed population is substantial.  ## Proof of Concept  ```text Environment: GitPython from the affected source tree; system git 2.43.0. The pulled origin uses a local filesystem transport (protocol.file.allow=always for git >= 2.38). ```  Reproduction steps:  1. Create an origin repository reachable over a local-path transport. 2. In a consumer repository, register that origin and call `Remote.pull()` with an attacker-controlled refspec. 3. Observe that the injected command executes.  ```python import git repo = git.Repo("consumer")                 # has an origin using a local-path or ssh transport origin = repo.remote("origin") # Attacker-controlled refspec value; default arguments (allow_unsafe_options=False): origin.pull(refspec="--upload-pack=touch /tmp/pwned; git-upload-pack") ```  ```text cmdline: git pull -v -- origin --upload-pack=touch /tmp/pwned; git-upload-pack [attack]  marker created (RCE)      : True [isolate] upload_pack passed as KWARG blocked : True   (only the positional refspec escapes) [sibling] same value via git fetch  : safe            (pull-specific behavior) [control] benign refspec            : safe ```  ## Attack Chain  1. **Exposure:** An application calls `Remote.pull(refspec=<value>)` on the default path, where `<value>` is derived from attacker-influenced input such as a branch or refspec request parameter. 2. **Control:** The attacker supplies the string `--upload-pack=<command>; git-upload-pack`. The value passes through `Git._unpack_args`, which only flattens and stringifies it, preserving the option shape. 3. **Path:** The protocol loop calls `Git.check_unsafe_protocols` on the value, which only matches remote-helper transport URLs (a `<transport>::` form) and does not flag an `--upload-pack=` token. 4. **Guard:** The unsafe-option guard calls `check_unsafe_options(options=Git._option_candidates([], kwargs), ...)`. Because positionals are passed as an empty list, the positional `refspec` is never inspected against `unsafe_git_pull_options`. 5. **Primitive:** The value is forwarded to `git pull -v -- <remote> --upload-pack=<command>; git-upload-pack`; `git pull` re-forwards the positional to an internal `git fetch` without a `--` separator, so it is honored as the upload-pack program. 6. **Result:** For a local-path or SSH transport, git executes `<command>` as the upload-pack program, giving arbitrary command execution as the calling process user.  ## Bypass Evidence  The relevant guard is `Remote.pull()`'s own `check_unsafe_options` call, present in the current released artifact. It is incomplete: it inspects `Git._option_candidates([], kwargs)`, which only considers keyword arguments, so the positional `refspec` is never checked. This was confirmed empirically: passing the identical value as the `upload_pack=` keyword argument raises `UnsafeOptionError`, while passing it as the positional `refspec` does not, proving that only the positional escapes the guard.  The `--` separator on the `git pull` command line was tested as a possible mitigation and refuted: with system git 2.43.0, `git pull -- <remote> '--upload-pack=<cmd>'` executed the injected command, while the identical value supplied to `git fetch -- ...` and `git push -- ...` did not execute, because those subcommands honor the `--` terminator whereas `git pull` re-forwards positionals to an internal fetch without one. The `check_unsafe_protocols` transport check was also examined and does not flag the `--upload-pack=` token because it has no `<transport>::` form. No prior published advisory for this package addresses `Remote.pull`, the fetch or pull refspec positional, or `--upload-pack` injection via a refspec; the closest accepted issue covers the same class (a positional argument escaping a keyword-only guard) in a different function and sink.  ## Affected Versions  - `Ecosystem: pip (PyPI)` - `Package: GitPython` - `Confirmed affected range: >= 3.1.30` - `Latest release checked: 3.1.62 (PyPI); source verified against the 3.1.62 release tag` - `Fix status: not fixed in any released version or on the development branch`  The keyword-only pull guard together with the positional `refspec` sink is present in every released tag from 3.1.30 through the latest release 3.1.62, verified by inspecting the shipped `git/remote.py` in each tagged artifact. Version 3.1.30 introduced the `unsafe_git_pull_options` guard; the affected range is stated from that boundary under the incomplete-guard framing. Releases before 3.1.30 forward the `refspec` positionally with no unsafe-option guard and no `--` separator and are also exploitable, but the range is stated conservatively from the guard-introduction boundary. No fixed release exists.  ## Suggested Fix  Enforce the unsafe-option invariant on the positional `refspec`, not only on keyword arguments. The guard should build its candidate list from the actual forwarded positionals (for example by passing the normalized refspec list into `Git._option_candidates` alongside `kwargs`) so that an option-shaped `refspec` such as `--upload-pack=...` is rejected with `UnsafeOptionError` unless `allow_unsafe_options=True`. The same correction should be verified for any other reference or refspec forwarding path that relies on the keyword-only guard. As an interim mitigation without a code change, callers should validate or reject refspec values that begin with `-`, avoid passing untrusted data as the `refspec`, and prefer HTTPS remotes where a client-supplied upload-pack program is inert.  Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

### Summary  This is a residual of GHSA-g5vv-9gxw-82hx / CVE-2026-87819. The 3.1.60 fix made `Actor._from_string` regex-free, but `parse_actor_and_date` still runs `_re_actor_epoch` on the same author/committer/tagger line one step earlier. That pattern backtracks quadratically when the trailing epoch or timezone is missing or malformed, so the same class of slow parse is still reachable in 3.1.62.  ### Details  `git/objects/util.py:322`:  ```python _re_actor_epoch = re.compile(r"^.+? (.*) (\d+) ([+-]\d+).*$") ```  `.+?` and `(.*)` can both absorb the same run of spaces, and the required ` (\d+) ([+-]\d+)` tail is only checked after them. On a long line with no valid tail, the search retries every split point.  It is called from `parse_actor_and_date` (`git/objects/util.py:335`), which runs on the author and committer lines in `Commit._deserialize` (`git/objects/commit.py:917`, `:931`) and on the tagger line in `git/objects/tag.py:129`.  The published payload (letters plus an unterminated `<`) is fast on 3.1.62. Replacing the letters with spaces is not:  | author line (after `author `) | 2 KB | 8 KB | 32 KB | |---|---|---|---| | `'a'*n + ' <'` (advisory payload) | 0.0 ms | 0.1 ms | 0.4 ms | | `' '*n` | 28 ms | 453 ms | 7,700 ms | | valid line, long name (control) | 0.0 ms | 0.0 ms | 0.0 ms |  Cost grows about 16x for each 4x increase in length.  ### PoC  ```python import time from git.objects.util import parse_actor_and_date  line = "author " + " " * 32000 t = time.perf_counter() parse_actor_and_date(line) print(f"{time.perf_counter() - t:.1f} s")   # ~7 s on 3.1.62 ```  End to end, reading `Commit.author` on a commit object whose author line is 32 KB of spaces followed by any malformed tail (no epoch, no timezone, non-numeric epoch, or bad timezone) takes about 7.2 s per access. The same line with a valid `1191999972 -0700` tail takes 1.3 ms.  Note for reproducing: `git hash-object -t commit -w` refuses such an object (`missingEmail`), so the test object was written with `--literally`. A remote can still serve one, because `fetch.fsckObjects` and `transfer.fsckObjects` default to false. This is the same delivery model as CVE-2026-87819 ("craft a commit object with a malformed author field").  ### Impact  CPU exhaustion (CWE-1333) in any application that uses GitPython to read commits or tags from an untrusted repository: CI tooling, repository scanners, code-hosting integrations. Each access to `Commit.author`, `Commit.committer` or `TagObject.tagger` on a crafted object costs seconds, and a repository can contain many such objects.  ### Suggested fix  Match the leading field name with `.[^ ]*` instead of `.+?`. Both stop at the first space after the first character, but `.[^ ]*` cannot overlap the following `(.*)`, so the backtracking disappears:  ```python _re_actor_epoch = re.compile(r"^.[^ ]* (.*) (\d+) ([+-]\d+).*$") _re_only_actor = re.compile(r"^.[^ ]* (.*)$") ```  Verification on current main (73a72c9):  - Differential over 368 actor lines (real-world shapes plus edge cases): 0 differences in match groups for either regex. - `' '*n` at 64 KB: 32,170 ms before, 0.98 ms after. Valid lines are unchanged (0.01 ms). - The existing test suite gives the same pass/fail set with and without the change - The new regression test, `test_parse_actor_and_date_malformed_line_is_linear`, fails on the old pattern (8.4 s) and passes with the fix (0.5 s).  The full patch (fix plus regression test) is attached below.  ```diff diff --git a/git/objects/util.py b/git/objects/util.py index a68d701f..d8c0594d 100644 --- a/git/objects/util.py +++ b/git/objects/util.py @@ -319,8 +319,11 @@ def parse_date(string_date: Union[str, datetime]) -> Tuple[int, int]:      # Precompiled regexes -_re_actor_epoch = re.compile(r"^.+? (.*) (\d+) ([+-]\d+).*$") -_re_only_actor = re.compile(r"^.+? (.*)$") +# The leading field name ("author", "committer", "tagger") is matched with ``.[^ ]*`` rather than +# ``.+?``: both stop at the first space after the first character, but ``.[^ ]*`` cannot overlap the +# following ``(.*)``, so a line with no valid trailing epoch/offset no longer backtracks quadratically. +_re_actor_epoch = re.compile(r"^.[^ ]* (.*) (\d+) ([+-]\d+).*$") +_re_only_actor = re.compile(r"^.[^ ]* (.*)$")      def parse_actor_and_date(line: str) -> Tuple[Actor, int, int]: diff --git a/test/test_util.py b/test/test_util.py index cf4299d5..e1631420 100644 --- a/test/test_util.py +++ b/test/test_util.py @@ -22,6 +22,7 @@ from git.cmd import dashify  from git.objects.util import (      altz_to_utctz_str,      from_timestamp, +    parse_actor_and_date,      parse_date,      tzoffset,      utctz_to_altz, @@ -571,6 +572,30 @@ class TestUtils(TestBase):              Actor("name last another", "some-very-long-email@example.com"),          )   +    def test_parse_actor_and_date_malformed_line_is_linear(self): +        # A long author line whose trailing epoch/offset is missing or malformed used to make +        # _re_actor_epoch backtrack quadratically: ~7 s per Commit.author access for a 32 KB line. +        # The parse result must be unchanged; only the time spent reaching it should move. +        for tail in ("", " notanumber -0700", " 1191999972", " -0700", " 1191999972 xx"): +            line = "author " + " " * 32000 + tail +            start = time.perf_counter() +            actor, epoch, offset = parse_actor_and_date(line) +            self.assertLess(time.perf_counter() - start, 1.0) +            self.assertEqual(epoch, 0) +            self.assertEqual(offset, 0) + +        # Well-formed lines, including one with a long name, still parse exactly as before. +        actor, epoch, offset = parse_actor_and_date( +            "author Tom Preston-Werner <tom@mojombo.com> 1191999972 -0700" +        ) +        self.assertEqual(actor, Actor("Tom Preston-Werner", "tom@mojombo.com")) +        self.assertEqual(epoch, 1191999972) +        self.assertEqual(offset, 25200) + +        actor, epoch, offset = parse_actor_and_date("author " + "a " * 16000 + "<a@b> 1 -0700") +        self.assertEqual(actor.email, "a@b") +        self.assertEqual(epoch, 1) +      @ddt.data(          ("name", ""),          ("name", "prefix_"), ```  Found with AI assistance (Claude) and verified by hand.
